So What Actually Is Microsoft Fabric?

A client we worked with last year was running four separate Azure services to handle what any reasonable engineer would describe as a single pipeline. Azure Data Factory for ingestion, Azure Synapse Analytics for transformation, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 for persistence, Power BI Premium for reporting. Four billing meters. Four access policy headaches. Four teams blaming each other when numbers on a dashboard looked wrong on a Tuesday morning. If none of that sounds familiar, you’re probably not the audience for this piece.

Microsoft Fabric is Microsoft’s answer to that specific kind of sprawl. Announced at Build 2023 and generally available since November 2023, it’s a unified SaaS analytics platform that folds most of those separate services into a single product with one governance layer, one capacity billing model, and one storage foundation underneath everything. Microsoft’s official description is “an end-to-end analytics platform,” which honestly undersells what actually changed at the architecture level. This is not a rebrand with a fresh coat of paint on the same internals. The storage model is genuinely different from what Synapse was doing.

OneLake is the thing worth paying attention to. Everything in Fabric writes to and reads from OneLake by default. One logical data lake scoped to your entire tenant, Delta Parquet format throughout, no copying data between workloads. That is the real shift. Not the UI consolidation, not the portal redesign.

The Core Components: What’s Inside Fabric

Fabric ships with what Microsoft calls “experiences,” each mapping to a different workload type. They share the same compute capacity and the same storage layer but present as distinct tools in the interface. Here is what you’re actually dealing with:

  • Data Factory – this is the Fabric-native version, not classic ADF. The pipeline canvas looks familiar enough that your existing engineers won’t be lost on day one, but Dataflow Gen2 is the more interesting piece since it runs Mashup (Power Query) at scale. Teams that already have substantial Power Query logic in their org tend to move faster here than they expect.
  • Synapse Data Engineering – Spark notebooks and Spark job definitions. Where your data engineers live when heavy transformation is on the table. One thing worth flagging: Spark clusters run against your Fabric capacity, so aggressively scheduled workloads during business hours will eat CUs fast. Cost modeling this in advance matters more than people give it credit for.
  • Synapse Data Warehousing – a serverless SQL endpoint sitting on top of OneLake. Write T-SQL, it reads Delta Parquet. No dedicated SQL pool to provision or babysit.
  • Synapse Real-Time Analytics – formerly Azure Data Explorer. Still KQL. Still Kusto under the hood. Most teams forget this exists right up until they need to handle streaming telemetry and then realize there’s already a capable engine sitting inside the capacity they’re already paying for.
  • Data Science – MLflow-integrated notebooks, experiment tracking, model registry. Honestly, still maturing as of mid-2024. I would not put a production ML pipeline here without going in with clear eyes about its current limitations.
  • Power BI – fully embedded, not bolted on as an afterthought. Direct Lake mode is the headline feature: semantic models read Delta files in OneLake at query time without import or DirectQuery overhead. This one actually delivers what the marketing promises.
  • Data Activator – reflex-based alerting that fires actions when data conditions cross defined thresholds. Early days, but the concept is legitimately useful for operational teams that need near-real-time responses without building custom event pipelines from scratch. Keep an eye on it.

OneLake sits under all of it. Think OneDrive but for structured and semi-structured analytical data. Every workspace gets a lakehouse or warehouse that maps to a folder structure in OneLake, and shortcuts let you reference external sources like ADLS Gen2, Amazon S3, or Google Cloud Storage without physically moving data. That shortcut feature alone has saved several clients from expensive data duplication patterns we saw repeatedly back in the Synapse era.

Microsoft Fabric vs. Legacy Azure Data Services: The Real Comparison

If you want to map what Fabric actually replaces versus what it doesn’t, the table below does more useful work than any high-level summary. Legacy tools are not disappearing tomorrow. But where Microsoft is putting its roadmap investment has clearly shifted, and that matters for long-term architectural decisions.

CapabilityLegacy Azure ToolMicrosoft Fabric EquivalentKey Difference
Orchestration / PipelinesAzure Data Factory (classic)Data Factory in FabricFabric version is SaaS-managed; no IR provisioning needed for cloud workloads
Big Data / SparkAzure Synapse Spark poolsSynapse Data Engineering (Fabric)Starter pools reduce cold-start delays; billing moves to capacity units
SQL AnalyticsSynapse Dedicated SQL PoolFabric Warehouse (serverless T-SQL)No provisioned DWUs; auto-scales against Fabric capacity units (CUs)
Storage LayerADLS Gen2 + manual Delta setupOneLake (Delta Parquet native)Delta format enforced by default; no separate storage account to manage
BI / ReportingPower BI Premium / EmbeddedPower BI in Fabric (Direct Lake)Direct Lake replaces both import and DirectQuery for Fabric lakehouses
Log / Telemetry AnalyticsAzure Data ExplorerReal-Time Analytics (KQL Database)Same Kusto engine, now billed through Fabric capacity instead of separately
ML / ExperimentationAzure Machine LearningData Science experience (MLflow)AML remains deeper for production ML; Fabric Data Science is still early-stage
GovernanceAzure Purview (separate resource)Microsoft Purview (integrated in Fabric)Unified catalog and sensitivity labels applied across all Fabric items

One honest caveat that doesn’t show up in any official migration guide: Azure Data Factory classic is not dead. If your environment has complex on-premises integration running on self-hosted Integration Runtime, Fabric’s pipeline experience is still catching up to that reality. We’ve seen migrations stall specifically on SSIS package compatibility and on-prem SQL Server sources that require self-hosted IR with specific network configurations. That gap is real and it’s not small. Plan for it before you commit to a timeline, not after you’ve already told your stakeholders it’s a six-week project.

Licensing: Capacity Units, SKUs, and What You’re Actually Paying For

This is where most enterprise evaluations run into trouble. Fabric does not use the old per-service billing model. You buy capacity measured in Capacity Units (CUs), and all workloads within that capacity share the pool. Microsoft calls this “Fabric capacity” and it’s purchasable two ways: directly through the Azure portal as pay-as-you-go or reserved instances, or via Microsoft 365 at F64 or above through certain enterprise agreements.

SKUCapacity Units (CUs)Approximate Monthly Cost (USD)Notes
F22 CUs~$263Dev/test only; no Power BI report sharing to free users
F44 CUs~$526Small workloads; Spark starter pools available at this tier
F88 CUs~$1,051Entry point for most small production scenarios
F3232 CUs~$4,205Mid-market enterprise workloads
F6464 CUs~$8,409Equivalent to Power BI Premium P1; unlocks Copilot features
F128128 CUs~$16,819Large enterprise; supports multiple workload teams on shared capacity

Pricing sourced from Microsoft’s official Fabric pricing page and will vary by region and EA discount tier.

The CU model looks clean on paper. Then you run a Spark job and a heavy Power BI refresh at the same time on a Monday morning. CU consumption spikes in a hurry. Fabric does have a built-in bursting mechanism that allows up to 10x your baseline CUs for short periods, which sounds generous until an F8 capacity gets throttled because the analytics team’s weekly refresh collided with a scheduled Spark pipeline. We watched this exact scenario play out in production. The Capacity Metrics app, a Fabric workbook you deploy separately, is not optional. Install it before you go live. Not on day ten after your first incident. Day one.

There’s also the per-user angle to keep in mind. End users consuming Power BI reports inside Fabric workspaces need either a Power BI Pro license or access via Fabric capacity at F64 and above, which covers report consumers within the tenant. Organizations already paying Power BI Premium Per Capacity usually find the migration math favors Fabric at F64 and above. But model it against your actual CU consumption patterns. Seat counts alone will give you the wrong answer every time.

Where Microsoft Fabric and Power BI Actually Intersect

The relationship between Fabric and Power BI is not really an integration story. Power BI is a native experience inside Fabric. Existing workspaces, datasets (now called semantic models), reports, and dataflows all live inside the Fabric umbrella already. If you’re using the Power BI service today, you’re already inside Fabric’s boundary in terms of the portal and workspace model. No migration required for that part.

The meaningful change for data engineers is Direct Lake mode. In classic Power BI you either import data into a compressed in-memory model, which gives you fast queries but data that ages out between refreshes, or you use DirectQuery, which gives you live data but slower queries and meaningful load on the source system. Direct Lake reads Delta Parquet files in OneLake directly at query time using a technique called “framing,” where the engine pins a consistent snapshot of the Delta log. Query performance lands close to import mode without the refresh cycle dependency. We tested this on a 400 million row fact table and the results were closer to import mode than we honestly expected. That said, relationship cardinality still matters quite a bit, and a poorly designed model will push you back toward DirectQuery behavior regardless of what storage mode you’re using.

For teams routing Dynamics 365 data through their analytics stack, the Dataverse shortcut in OneLake is worth knowing about. You can create a shortcut from a Fabric lakehouse directly to Dataverse tables, surfacing Dynamics data in OneLake without a separate export pipeline. It’s not full write-back. But for reporting on Dynamics data alongside other enterprise sources, it removes a layer of complexity that previously required configuring Azure Synapse Link for Dataverse, which was not a trivial setup for most teams.

Practical Advice Before You Commit to Fabric

Start with an F8 or F16 in a non-production environment and deploy the Capacity Metrics app on day one. Not day ten. You need actual CU consumption data before you have any basis for sizing a production capacity, and nothing else gives you that visibility out of the box.

The OneLake shortcut to ADLS Gen2 is your best friend during migration. You do not need to move all existing data into Fabric lakehouse storage immediately. Point shortcuts at your current Gen2 containers, validate that pipelines and SQL queries behave correctly against them, then migrate gradually. Teams that attempt a full cutover in one move consistently run into Delta table format compatibility issues with older data that was written by Synapse Spark without proper Delta log cleanup. Vacuum your Delta tables before pointing Fabric at them. This one bites people more often than it should, and it is entirely avoidable with a bit of prep work.

On the governance side, if your org already uses Microsoft Purview, the integration is in reasonably good shape. Sensitivity labels applied in Purview propagate into Fabric items, and lineage tracking across pipelines, lakehouses, and semantic models surfaces in one catalog view. Microsoft’s documentation on Purview and Fabric governance is worth reading carefully before you finalize your workspace and domain structure, because some of those decisions are genuinely difficult to undo after the fact.

And this is blunt: Fabric is not the right answer if most of your workload is transactional processing. It’s an analytics platform. Full stop. If someone on your team is suggesting Fabric as a replacement for Azure SQL Database or as an application backend, that conversation needs to be corrected before it turns into a bad architecture you’re stuck maintaining.

FAQ

What is Microsoft Fabric and how is it different from Azure Synapse Analytics?

Microsoft Fabric is a unified SaaS analytics platform that brings Data Factory, Synapse Data Engineering, a SQL warehouse, Real-Time Analytics, Power BI, and Data Science experiences together under one product and one billing model. Azure Synapse Analytics was a partially integrated PaaS offering where storage, compute, and linked services were still configured and managed separately. The core architectural difference is OneLake: a single tenant-wide Delta Parquet storage layer that all Fabric workloads share natively, which eliminates the need to copy or move data between compute engines.

Can you use Microsoft Fabric with existing Power BI reports and semantic models?

Yes, and this transition is smoother than most people expect. Power BI is a native experience inside Fabric, so existing workspaces, reports, and semantic models are accessible within the Fabric portal without any migration steps. The new capability Fabric adds is Direct Lake mode, which lets semantic models query Delta Parquet files in OneLake at near-import-mode speed without a scheduled refresh cycle sitting in between. Existing import and DirectQuery models continue working exactly as before, so there’s no forced change to your current setup.

What Fabric SKU should a mid-market enterprise start with?

For a first production deployment covering a moderate number of pipelines, a data warehouse or lakehouse, and Power BI reporting for an internal analytics team, F32 or F64 is usually the right starting range. F64 is worth serious consideration if you want Copilot features or need Fabric capacity to cover Power BI report consumption without assigning Pro licenses per user. That said, run an F8 or F16 in dev first, deploy the Capacity Metrics app, and watch actual CU burn rates for a few weeks before making a production sizing decision. Let real usage data drive that call rather than a spreadsheet estimate built on assumptions about how your workloads will behave.
